raw_case_text: A 21-year-old male presented with fever, cough, anorexia and weight loss of 2 months duration. He was a student, did not smoke and did not report alcohol or substance abuse. He did not have any significant medical history and was immunized appropriately. He reported exposure to pulmonary tuberculosis as a caregiver to a sibling 18 months prior to this episode; his sister recovered completely with 6 months of antituberculosis treatment. Tuberculin testing or isoniazid prophylaxis was not offered to the index patient according to current practice in India. He did not raise pets and had stayed alone in a hostel for the last 4 months. Chest radiographs showed bilateral infiltrates and computed tomography [CT, Figure 1] showed findings suggestive of extensive pulmonary tuberculosis. Tuberculin skin testing was negative (6 mm with 5 TU at 72 h). Sputum smears were strongly positive for acid-fast bacilli by Zeihl-Neelsen's stain and supervised daily four-drug antituberculosis treatment (isoniazid 200 mg, rifampicin 450 mg, pyrazinamide 1000 mg, ethambutol 600 mg, pyridoxine 20 mg; weight 40 kg) was initiated and sputum cultures and drug susceptibility for Mycobacterium tuberculosis by multiple growth indicator technique (MGIT) was requested. Sputum for GeneXpert for M. tuberculosis did not show resistance to rifampicin. Nutrition counseling and four doses of 2-weekly Vitamin D 100,000 I.U were administered as per unit's protocol. He presented with fever, worsening breathlessness, weight loss and chest pain 4 weeks after starting treatment. On examination he was afebrile, normotensive with respiratory rate of 40 breaths/min and pulse rate of 130 beats/min. He was malnourished (body mass inde x 14 kg/m2, normal 19-25 kg/m2). Respiratory examination showed reduced right-sided movements and breath sound intensity with coarse left-sided crackles. Resting SpO2 was 80%. Chest radiography [Figure 1, left] confirmed the diagnosis of right-sided pneumothorax with increased bilateral infiltrates. He was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) with appropriate respiratory isolation; intercostal chest drain was inserted on the right side. There was evidence of air-leak (Cerfolio E) from the right lung with minimal subcutaneous emphysema. Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) was started; no worsening of air-leak was noted. Repeat sputum smears showed downgrading of smears with scanty acid-fast bacilli by Zeihl-Neelsen's stain. Sputum cultures requested at treatment onset confirmed pan-sensitive M. tuberculosis. Repeat CT-chest [Figure 2] showed increase in cavitation, consolidation and ground-glass opacities bilaterally. Further investigations are summarized in Table 1. Fasting blood glucose was 87 mg/dL and human immunodeficiency virus ELISA was negative and there was no CD4 lymphocytopenia. Sputum smears for Pneumocystis jirovecii were negative. Urine microscopy was normal and negative for albuminuria. Arterial blood gas analysis showed corrected hypoxemia and respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.42, PO2 78 mm Hg on FiO20.4, PCO228 mm Hg, HCO322 mEq/L). Quantiferon-TB GOLD in-tube assay was strongly positive. He was continued on four-drug antituberculosis treatment; further doses of Vitamin D were not administered. He developed contralateral pneumothorax on the 2nd day of admission and worsened hypoxemia needing mechanical ventilation. Urgent left intercostal tube drainage was performed and air-leak (Cerfolio I) was noticed on the left side also. Repeat MGIT tuberculosis cultures were reported negative by day 10 of ICU admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old male student with smear-positive, pan-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis presented 4 weeks after initiating four-drug antituberculosis therapy and high-dose vitamin D supplementation with fever, worsening breathlessness, weight loss, and acute chest pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with a 2-month history of fever, cough, anorexia, and weight loss 18 months after serving as caregiver to a sister with pulmonary tuberculosis. Baseline chest imaging showed extensive bilateral infiltrates, sputum Ziehl-Neelsen smears were strongly positive for acid-fast bacilli (GeneXpert rifampicin-susceptible), and he was started on supervised daily weight-based four-drug antituberculosis therapy (isoniazid 200 mg, rifampicin 450 mg, pyrazinamide 1,000 mg, ethambutol 600 mg, pyridoxine 20 mg; weight 40 kg) plus four biweekly oral doses of 100,000 IU vitamin D. Four weeks into treatment, he presented with recurrent fever, severe worsening breathlessness, chest pain, and weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Smear- and culture-positive pan-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis diagnosed 4 weeks prior; household tuberculosis contact (cared for his sister with pulmonary TB 18 months earlier without receiving latent TB prophylaxis). Nonsmoker, student living in a hostel, no alcohol or substance abuse, immunized appropriately.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, worsening breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, anorexia, and severe weight loss. Home medications were isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, pyridoxine, and biweekly high-dose vitamin D (100,000 IU).

objective.physical_examination: At 4-week readmission: Afebrile and normotensive, severe malnutrition with weight 40 kg and BMI 14 kg/m2 (normal: 19–25 kg/m2), marked tachypnea (respiratory rate 40 breaths/min), tachycardia (pulse 130 beats/min), and severe resting hypoxemia (SpO2 80%). Chest examination: Reduced right-sided chest wall movement and diminished right breath sounds with coarse left-sided crackles (followed on ICU day 2 by contralateral left-sided pneumothorax).
objective.routine_investigations: Arterial blood gas (on FiO2 0.40): pH 7.42, PaO2 78 mmHg, PaCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3- 22 mEq/L. Laboratory tests: Fasting blood glucose 87 mg/dL, HIV ELISA negative, normal urinalysis without albuminuria; baseline tuberculin skin test anergic (6 mm at 72 h), while QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube assay at readmission was strongly positive. Sputum studies: Baseline strongly AFB-positive sputum downgraded at 4 weeks to scanty AFB; baseline MGIT culture confirmed pan-sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and repeat MGIT cultures turned negative by ICU day 10; sputum smears for Pneumocystis jirovecii were negative. Chest radiographs: Right-sided spontaneous pneumothorax with increased bilateral infiltrates on readmission, followed by contralateral left-sided pneumothorax on ICU day 2.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological workup: Normal CD4+ T-lymphocyte count (no CD4 lymphocytopenia). Repeat chest CT at 4-week readmission: Marked paradoxical progression of bilateral cavitation, consolidation, and ground-glass opacities compared to baseline.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Paradoxical tuberculous immune reconstitution / paradoxical reaction (potentiated by high-dose vitamin D supplementation and manifested by conversion from tuberculin anergy to a strongly positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold assay, worsening bilateral cavitary/ground-glass infiltrates, and sequential bilateral life-threatening spontaneous pneumothoraces) in an HIV-negative young adult with pan-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis; Pneumocystis jirovecii co-infection was excluded by negative sputum smears and normal CD4 counts. Plan and clinical course: Managed in the ICU with right intercostal tube drainage (for Cerfolio grade E air leak) and noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation, followed on ICU day 2 by urgent left intercostal tube drainage (for Cerfolio grade I air leak) and invasive mechanical ventilation. Further doses of vitamin D were discontinued while standard four-drug antituberculosis therapy was continued, achieving negative MGIT sputum cultures by ICU day 10.
